title: Benefits of Physical Exercise for the Mother, Fetus, Newborn, and Infant
summary:
The chapter argues that older advice to rest during pregnancy has been replaced by evidence that moderate exercise, and in some cases well-supervised higher-intensity exercise, is safe and beneficial in most low-risk pregnancies. Pregnancy is presented as a window of opportunity to build lasting healthy habits.

For mothers, exercise is linked to fewer cesareans, less gestational diabetes, preeclampsia and gestational hypertension, less excessive weight gain, better mood and sleep, and less back and pelvic pain. For newborns it is linked to healthy birth weight, better Apgar scores and shorter hospital stays. Infant studies suggest benefits for motor and neurodevelopment and lower obesity risk, though some studies at ages 7 and 18 months found no differences. The authors conclude that prenatal exercise in women without contraindications should be part of routine obstetric care, with personalization and supervision.
points: Moderate exercise, and in some cases well-supervised higher-intensity exercise, is safe and beneficial in most low-risk pregnancies.
Maternal benefits include fewer cesarean deliveries, lower risk of gestational diabetes, preeclampsia and gestational hypertension, and less excessive gestational weight gain.
Exercise also reduces depressive symptoms, back and pelvic pain, fatigue and stress, improves sleep, helps prevent and manage urinary incontinence, and reduces postpartum weight retention.
Lack of exercise during pregnancy increases the risk of a macrosomic fetus by 2.5 times.
Newborns of active mothers have lower fat mass at birth, better Apgar scores and shorter neonatal hospital stays.
Excess birth weight raises risks such as hypoglycemia and shoulder dystocia, while birth weight under 2500 g is linked to developmental complications and later chronic disease.
At 5 days, 1 month and 1 year, studies report better neurobehavioral capacity, lower adiposity, higher heart rate variability and better neuromotor development in children of exercising mothers.
At age 7 there was no association between maternal exercise and child weight or neurodevelopment, and one study found no motor skill difference at 18 months.
The most recent evidence (2020-2025) confirms exercise in women without contraindications is safe, with no increased risk of preterm birth.
takeaways: Treat pregnancy as a chance to establish exercise habits that may last a lifetime.
Regular exercise is a practical tool for gestational weight control and lowering the risk of gestational diabetes and hypertension.
Include pelvic floor training to help prevent and manage urinary incontinence.
Expect mood, sleep, and back and pelvic pain to benefit from staying active.
Exercise can help keep birth weight in a healthy range, which matters for both the mother and the baby.
Personalize and supervise the program, and treat prenatal exercise as part of routine obstetric care.
cautions: The benefits apply to women without contraindications and in low-risk pregnancies.
Higher-intensity exercise is only described as acceptable when well supervised.
